content: Traumatic eye injuries account for approximately 3% of all visits to hospital emergency departments. Among these, blunt trauma is the most common type of injury, responsible for 30% of such cases. Blunt trauma to the eye often results in a condition known as traumatic iridocyclitis, which is a form of anterior uveitis. This condition is characterized by symptoms such as excessive tearing, sensitivity to light (photophobia), eye pain, and potential vision loss. These symptoms arise due to inflammation and spasms in the ciliary muscles, which affect the iris and its sphincter. The standard treatment for the inflammatory component of traumatic iridocyclitis involves the use of topical corticosteroids. To address the ciliary muscle spasms, topical mydriatic agents are often employed as an adjunctive therapy. These agents work by dilating the pupil, thereby reducing the spasms. However, the effectiveness of mydriatic agents in alleviating ocular pain and preventing vision loss has not been clearly quantified. The objective of this study was to assess the efficacy and safety of using topical mydriatic agents as an adjunctive treatment alongside topical corticosteroids for managing traumatic iridocyclitis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL Plus, PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). No restrictions were applied regarding the date or language of the studies. The last search was performed on June 12, 2019. The inclusion criteria for this review specified randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared the combination of topical mydriatic agents and corticosteroids with corticosteroids alone in patients diagnosed with traumatic iridocyclitis. Two independent reviewers screened the titles, abstracts, and full-text articles to determine eligibility. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion. The plan was to extract data independently from the included studies. However, no eligible RCTs were identified that met the inclusion criteria. As a result, there is no evidence from RCTs to support or refute the efficacy of topical mydriatic agents as an adjunctive therapy to corticosteroids for the treatment of traumatic iridocyclitis. In the absence of such studies, no definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding their effectiveness or safety. To address this gap in evidence, well-designed controlled trials are needed. These studies should compare the combined use of topical mydriatic agents and corticosteroids with the use of corticosteroids alone in patients with traumatic iridocyclitis. Such research could provide valuable insights into the potential benefits and risks of using mydriatic agents as an adjunctive treatment for this condition.
